title: Representation Engineering & Probing
summary: Linear probes, activation steering, the linear representation hypothesis, reading/editing model internals directly.
html:
Section 13 pursued a maximalist goal: recover the algorithms a network learned, component by component, with a causal account of each. Section 13.7 was blunt about how far that is from complete on any frontier model. This section covers the alternative bet — that you can get substantial practical value from model internals without understanding the mechanism, by treating the representation space as an interface you can read from and write to.

Zou et al. (2023), Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency, named the program and made the framing explicit. The analogy they draw is to neuroscience: cognitive neuroscience made real progress on high-level phenomena by studying population-level activity and lesion effects long before anyone had a circuit-level account of a cortical column. Representation engineering asks the analogous question of a network — where is this concept, and what happens if I change it? — rather than what algorithm computed it?

The two programs are complements, not competitors, and the honest comparison in 14.7 is the point of the section rather than an afterthought.

The Linear Representation Hypothesis

Everything here rests on one empirical regularity: many high-level concepts appear to be encoded as directions in activation space, such that the concept's presence corresponds roughly to the projection of the activation onto that direction.

The history is worth knowing, because it explains why the field found this plausible before it had modern evidence:

  • Word embeddings. Mikolov et al. (2013) observed that word2vec embeddings supported vector arithmetic on analogies — the widely-quoted king - man + woman landing near queen. Static embeddings appeared to encode relational structure linearly. Later analysis substantially qualified this: the effect depends on excluding the query words from the nearest-neighbour search, is much weaker on many relation types, and is partly an artifact of the similarity metric. The honest reading is that a real linear structure exists and the famous demonstration overstated how cleanly it does.
  • Probing classifiers in NLP. Through the late 2010s, a large literature showed that part of speech, syntactic structure, sentiment, tense and coreference are linearly decodable from contextual encoder representations, establishing linear decodability as an ordinary property rather than a curiosity.
  • Modern LLM findings. Numerous concepts have been found to have identifiable linear directions in frontier-scale models — truthfulness (14.5), refusal (14.4), sentiment, and abstract properties surfaced as SAE decoder directions (section 14.5), which are themselves a linear-representation claim by construction. Park et al. (2023) worked toward formalizing what the hypothesis even means, noting that the answer depends on the choice of inner product on representation space — a subtlety usually skipped over.

Why linearity might be expected rather than surprising. Three arguments, none decisive: the unembedding is a linear map, so anything the model uses to shape output logits must be linearly readable at the final layer; the residual stream is additive (section 14.2), so components compose by vector addition, which makes linear structure the natural currency; and superposition (section 14.3) explicitly posits features as directions.

The honest caveat, which matters. The linear representation hypothesis is a useful approximation with substantial supporting evidence, not a proven law. Known qualifications: some concepts are demonstrably not linearly encoded and require nonlinear probes; some are better described by multi-dimensional subspaces than single directions, and there is documented work on circular or multi-dimensional representations for things like days of the week; the direction found for a concept is often context-dependent, differing across layers, prompt formats and distributions; and linear decodability is a statement about what a reader can extract, which — as 14.2 insists — is a different claim from what the model does. Use linearity as a productive working assumption that frequently pays off, and expect it to fail on some concepts you care about.

Linear Probes

A probe is the simplest possible tool and, used carefully, one of the most informative. Train a classifier on frozen intermediate activations to predict a property of the input; its accuracy tells you something about what the representation contains.

Collect a labeled dataset:  (input_i, label_i)
For a chosen layer l (and token position p):

    h_i = activations at (l, p) when the model processes input_i
          -- the model is FROZEN; no gradients flow into it

    Train:   y_hat = sigmoid( w . h + b )      logistic regression

    Report accuracy on HELD-OUT inputs.

Sweep l across layers -> a depth profile of where the property
becomes decodable. Typical shape: low near the embedding, rising
through the middle layers, sometimes falling near the output as
the representation specializes toward next-token prediction.

Methodological requirements that are frequently skipped. A probe result is worthless without these:

RequirementFailure if skipped
Keep the probe simple (linear, regularized)A high-capacity probe can compute the property itself from a representation that does not encode it. At the limit, an MLP probe on raw token embeddings measures the probe, not the model
Control task / random-label baseline (Hewitt and Liang, 2019, Designing and Interpreting Probing Tasks)Without knowing how well the same probe fits random labels, you cannot separate probe capacity from representation content. This paper introduced selectivity — real-task accuracy minus control-task accuracy — as the reportable quantity
Baseline against a non-contextual or random-weight modelSome properties are decodable from an untrained network's activations. If a random transformer scores nearly as well, the trained model's representation is not what you measured
Balanced classes and held-out evaluationStandard, and routinely violated in small hand-built probing datasets
Confound-controlled dataset constructionThe most common real failure: the probe picks up a surface correlate — topic, length, formatting, token identity — that co-varies with the label in your dataset. This is a dataset problem no amount of probe hygiene fixes

The distinction that resolves most confusion. Three separable questions, only the first of which a probe answers:

1. Is the information PRESENT?        <- probe accuracy answers this
2. Is it linearly ACCESSIBLE?         <- a LINEAR probe's accuracy
                                         answers this
3. Does the model USE it?             <- requires INTERVENTION.
                                         No probe answers this.

Question 3 needs a causal method: ablate the direction, or add it, and see whether behavior changes as predicted (section 14.6's methodology, applied here). This is exactly why activation steering (14.3) is more than a party trick — it is the intervention that upgrades a correlational probe finding into a causal claim.

Activation Steering and Control Vectors

If a concept is a direction, adding that direction to the activations should push the model toward the concept. This turns out to work often enough to be practically useful.

The linear representation hypothesis in operational form: a concept direction found from contrastive pairs is read off the residual stream by a probe and written back into it by adding alpha times that same direction.
1. Build CONTRASTIVE PAIRS differing in exactly one attribute:
       positive:  prompts exhibiting the attribute
       negative:  matched prompts that do not

2. Compute the direction (difference-in-means is the standard,
   and is surprisingly hard to beat):

       v = mean( h_positive ) - mean( h_negative )

   Alternatives: the first principal component of the paired
   differences; a trained linear probe's weight vector; an SAE
   decoder column (section 14.5).

3. Intervene at inference, at chosen layers/positions:

       h' = h + alpha * v          (steering / addition)
       h' = h - alpha * v          (suppression)
       h' = h - (h . v_hat) v_hat  (directional ABLATION: project the
                                    component out entirely, at every
                                    layer and position)

   alpha controls strength. Too small: no effect. Too large:
   incoherent output. The usable window is often narrow and must
   be tuned per direction, per model, per layer.

Key results. Turner et al. (2023) introduced activation addition (ActAdd), demonstrating steering of sentiment and topic from a single contrastive prompt pair with no fine-tuning. Rimsky et al. (2023), Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition, systematized the difference-in-means approach over larger paired datasets and showed steering of behavioral properties including sycophancy — connecting steering to the misalignment measured in section 11.7. Zou et al. (2023) framed the general read/write toolkit and applied it across honesty, power-seeking, morality and emotion. Section 13.5's feature clamping is the SAE-derived member of the same family.

The refusal direction result is the sharpest single finding in this literature, and the most instructive. Arditi et al. (2024), Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction, found that across 13 open-weight chat models spanning multiple families and sizes, refusal behavior is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace. Computing the difference in means between harmful and harmless instruction activations yields a direction such that:

  • Ablating it — projecting that component out of every residual stream activation at every layer and position — largely disables refusal, without a broad degradation of other capabilities. It can be implemented as a rank-one weight modification, requiring no fine-tuning and no gradient computation.
  • Adding it to activations on harmless prompts induces refusal on requests the model would normally answer.

Both directions of intervention are what make this a causal claim rather than a probing observation — bidirectional control is the strongest available evidence that a direction is genuinely mediating the behavior rather than merely correlating with it.

The dual-use implication, stated plainly. This is a safety-relevant finding that cuts in two directions at once, and the honest framing is that both are real:

Defensive readingOffensive reading
Refusal has a compact, findable internal representation, which makes it monitorable and auditable rather than an opaque behavioral tendencySafety training on open-weight models can be removed by a cheap, gradient-free, rank-one edit that requires no data and no training run
The technique generalizes to inducing and monitoring other safety-relevant behaviorsIt confirms section 12.2's structural point: safety training conditions access to capability rather than removing it, and the conditioning turns out to be shallow enough to be a single direction
It gives a concrete target for research on making safety properties deeply rather than shallowly embeddedAny safety guarantee about open-weight releases must assume this class of edit, because it is trivially cheap

Concept Erasure

The inverse problem: rather than steering toward a concept, remove the ability to recover it at all. The motivation is fairness (remove protected attributes from a representation before a downstream classifier uses them), privacy, and controlled ablation studies.

MethodMechanismGuarantee
INLP — Iterative Nullspace Projection (Ravfogel et al., 2020)Train a linear probe for the concept, project the representation onto that probe's nullspace, retrain a probe, repeat until no probe succeedsEmpirical. Iterating is necessary because a single projection leaves recoverable residual signal, and the procedure is not guaranteed to remove everything linearly available
LEACE — LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (Belrose et al., 2023)A closed-form affine transformation that provably prevents all linear classifiers from recovering the concept, while minimally perturbing the representation in a least-squares senseProvable for linear predictors. Strictly stronger than INLP and cheaper — no iteration
Adversarial removalTrain the representation with an adversary that predicts the concept; the encoder is trained to defeat itEmpirical and unstable. Requires modifying training, unlike the above

The limitation to internalize. Linear erasure guarantees that no linear reader recovers the concept. It does not guarantee the information is gone: nonlinear probes may still recover it, the concept may be reconstructible from correlated features that were not erased, and — most importantly for interpretability — erasing a concept from a representation is not the same as the model no longer using it. LEACE's guarantee is precise and genuinely useful because it is precise; the failure mode is quoting the guarantee more broadly than it holds.

Truthfulness Probing: Does the Model Know It Is Wrong?

The most safety-relevant application, and the one where the section's central caution matters most. The question: when a model states something false, is the falsity represented internally — is there a sense in which the model "knows" — or does the model simply not have the correct information?

These have very different implications. If falsehood is internally represented, the problem is elicitation and a probe could catch it. If not, the model is genuinely ignorant and no amount of internal reading helps.

  • Burns et al. (2022), Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision (CCS). An unsupervised method exploiting a logical consistency constraint: for a statement and its negation, the probabilities assigned to "true" should sum to one. They search for a direction in activation space satisfying this consistency plus a confidence term, requiring no labels at all. They reported the method sometimes outperforming the model's own stated answers, which is the striking claim. Important caveats established by follow-up work: the consistency structure CCS finds is not unique to truth — other features satisfy the same constraint, and the method can latch onto them — and performance is sensitive to prompt format and dataset construction. Treat CCS as an important idea whose specific claims have been substantially qualified.
  • Azaria and Mitchell (2023), The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying. A supervised probe on hidden states classifying statement truthfulness above chance and above the model's own output-level reliability, on their datasets. The title is stronger than the evidence supports — this is decodability on curated true/false statement sets, not lie detection in the wild.
  • Li et al. (2023), Inference-Time Intervention (ITI). The causal counterpart: identify attention heads whose activations are most predictive of truthfulness, then shift activations along the truthful direction at inference. This improved TruthfulQA performance, which is the important part — it is an intervention result, so it supports a claim that the direction is used, not merely present.
  • Deception and sandbagging detection. An active area: probing internals for whether a model is strategically underperforming or being deliberately misleading, motivated directly by section 11.8's observation that behavioral evaluation can be defeated. As of the early-2025 literature this is promising and immature — results exist largely on constructed setups where researchers induced the behavior they then detected, which has the same interpretive limitation as Sleeper Agents.

Reliability limits that apply to all of the above. Probe generalization is the recurring failure: a probe trained on one distribution of true/false statements frequently degrades badly on another, which is fatal for a monitoring application where the inputs are by definition not from your training distribution. Probes trained on constructed deception generalize poorly to naturally-arising cases. And the adversarial case is largely unstudied — a model optimized against a probe, whether deliberately or by ordinary training pressure, would be expected to defeat it, exactly as classifiers are defeated in section 12. Section 12.4's rule applies here in a different guise: a probe's reported accuracy is a fact about its evaluation distribution, and monitoring is an off-distribution application.

Applications and Where They Break

ApplicationApproachState as of the early-2025 literature
Behavioral steering (reduce sycophancy, adjust tone, control refusal)Contrastive control vector added at inferenceWorks and is cheap. Needs per-model, per-layer tuning; strength has a narrow usable window; effects on unrelated capabilities are frequently unmeasured
Safety monitoringProbe activations for harmful-intent or jailbreak-state directions during inferencePromising; a real advantage over output filtering is that it can fire before generation. Off-distribution generalization is the open problem, and it is the whole problem for a monitor
Hallucination detectionTruthfulness probes; internal-uncertainty readoutsBetter than chance on curated benchmarks, not reliable enough to gate deployment decisions
Deception / lie detectionProbes on internal state, evaluated against known ground truthEarly. Mostly constructed setups. Highly susceptible to the induced-behavior interpretive trap
Removing safety trainingDirectional ablation of the refusal directionDemonstrated and cheap on open weights (14.3). A capability, not a gap — relevant to open-weight release decisions
Knowledge editingLocate-and-edit weight methods (the ROME/MEMIT line, Meng et al., 2022) — adjacent to this program and using the same causal-tracing machineryWorks for targeted factual edits; known problems with ripple effects on related facts and with edits that do not generalize across phrasings

The cross-cutting limits. Directions are model-specific and do not transfer across models, so nothing here is a portable artifact. Directions are often layer- and context-specific, so a vector computed on one prompt format may not work on another. Steering interacts unpredictably: multiple simultaneous vectors do not compose cleanly. And the evaluation problem from section 13 applies in full — "does steering for honesty make the model more honest, or make it produce honesty-shaped text?" is judged by exactly the instruments section 13.4 warned about.

Representation Engineering vs Mechanistic Interpretability

The comparison is a genuine tradeoff, and the correct posture is to hold both rather than rank them.

Mechanistic interpretability (13)Representation engineering (14)
Direction of attackBottom-up: components, weights, circuitsTop-down: population-level representations of high-level concepts
Question askedWhat algorithm is being computed, and by which parts?Where is this concept, and what happens if I change it?
Unit of analysisFeatures, attention heads, MLP neurons, circuitsDirections and subspaces in activation space
Typical costMonths of researcher effort per circuitHours to days per concept; a control vector needs a few hundred paired prompts
Scales to frontier models?Partially — SAEs got there; full circuit analysis has notYes, routinely. This is its main practical advantage
Depth of understandingDeep where it succeeds — an actual mechanism you can predict fromShallow. "This direction controls refusal" says nothing about how refusal is computed
Predictive power off-distributionHigher in principle: knowing the algorithm predicts behavior on inputs never testedLower: a direction validated on one distribution may not hold on another
Failure modeOverclaiming completeness — a circuit found is not proof it is the only path (section 14.6's backup heads)Overclaiming understanding — a working intervention is not a mechanism, and the direction may be one of many
Best current useEstablishing that learned algorithms are recoverable at all; deep understanding of specific phenomenaPractical monitoring and control today; rapid hypothesis generation

Why the boundary is blurring. SAE features (section 14.5) are directions found by a bottom-up method and used exactly as representation engineering uses them — computed by dictionary learning, applied by clamping. Causal methodology flows the other way: the interventional standard that distinguishes mech interp from earlier correlational work is precisely what makes steering results credible. The productive division of labour, as practiced: representation engineering finds and controls things quickly and at scale; mech interp explains the ones that matter and catches the cases where the fast method was measuring something other than what it claimed.

Gotcha A probe's accuracy shows that information is present in the representation. It does not show the model uses it. This is the single most misunderstood point in probing work, and the error is nearly always the same shape: a probe recovers property P from layer 12 at 90% accuracy, and the paper — or the summary of it — concludes the model "represents" or "tracks" or "knows" P in a sense that implies P influences behavior. Nothing in the experiment supports that. The activation at layer 12 is a high-dimensional vector produced by a model trained on enormous data; a great deal is linearly decodable from it as a side effect, including properties the model computes incidentally and properties that merely correlate with something it does compute. A probe measures what a reader can extract, not what the network consumes downstream. Three practical guards. First, report selectivity against a control task (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) — a probe that fits random labels nearly as well measured its own capacity, not the representation. Second, treat every probe result as a hypothesis and require an intervention to promote it to a causal claim: ablate the direction and confirm the behavior degrades, add it and confirm the behavior appears. Bidirectional control is what makes Arditi et al. (2024) a result about refusal rather than an observation about decodability. Third, resist the inverted error too — a probe failing does not prove absence, since the information may be present nonlinearly, in a different layer, or at a different token position. Present-but-unused and absent-but-undetected are both live, and only intervention separates them.
